title: "O my father"
hookLine: Ibrahim pleads with his father gently four times, and parts with, peace be upon you (19:41–47)

lines: HOW THE SON LEAVES THE ROOM.
cards: Politics at the holiday table. A career. A marriage.

Faith. An argument with a parent about something that matters can start calm and end with someone leaving the room. Surah Maryam has one of these conversations, between a young man and his father, and the subject is God.
It starts calm and ends badly. But the way the son leaves the room is the whole lesson. Listen for how he begins each sentence.

teach.b: The son is Ibrahim. His father, named Azar in another surah, makes and serves idols.

teach.h: FOUR PLEAS, THE LAST ONE FEAR.
teach.b: Ibrahim begins each of his four sentences the same way: ya abati. O my father. Grammarians note that this form of address is tender, something like my dear father.
One: my father, why worship what can't hear, can't see, and can't help you at all? Two: my father, knowledge has come to me that hasn't come to you, so follow me, and I'll guide you on a level road.
Three: my father, don't serve Shaytan. Four: my father, I'm afraid a punishment from the Merciful will touch you. The fourth isn't a threat.
It's fear for him. Then the father answers: do you turn away from my gods, Ibrahim? If you don't stop, I'll stone you.
Get away from me for a long time. Plenty of arguments end right there. Ibrahim's reply, in Pickthall's words, begins: "Peace be unto thee!"
Salamun 'alayk. Then: I'll ask my Lord to forgive you; He has always been kind to me.

teach.h: I'LL STONE YOU. GET AWAY FROM ME.
teach.b: And: I'll withdraw from you and from what you call on, and I'll call on my Lord.
He leaves without slamming the door, and without giving up his conviction. Both are true at once.
The Qur'an is honest that the story goes further: At-Tawbah says that later, when it became clear his father was set against God, Ibrahim dissociated himself from him.
But in this moment, threatened with stoning, he answers with peace, and a promise to pray.

how: Muslim teachers cite Ibrahim's words in 19:42–47 as the model for speaking to parents who don't share one's faith: gently, respectfully, and without abandoning conviction.

o: my father's gods, the idols Azar served
O my dear father, a tender way to address him
O my lord, said to a king in respect

games.q: inside the conversation — tap the pairs.
p: the father's name, in another surah

s: Ibrahim's fourth plea is a threat of punishment
it's fear for his father: I'm afraid a punishment will touch you.
Ibrahim parts from his father with peace and a promise to pray
19:47: peace be upon you; I'll ask my Lord to forgive you.
the Qur'an says nothing more about Ibrahim and his father
At-Tawbah 9:114 says he later dissociated himself once his father's enmity to God was clear.

games.q: your father says: stop, or I'll stone you; get away from me. what do you say as you go, as Ibrahim?
o: peace be upon you; I'll ask my Lord to forgive you.
games.why: salamun 'alayk, and a promise to pray for him. he leaves without giving up his conviction, and without slamming the door.

practice: Bring to mind a disagreement you're in with someone close, and how it last ended. Now picture yourself at the end of that conversation doing what Ibrahim did: keeping your view, and still leaving with peace.
Find the words that are yours: peace be with you, I'll keep you in my prayers, I love you and I see it differently.

wordCard.voice: Ya abati. O my father: Ibrahim's tender address, four times, to a father who threatened him, ending with peace. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: O my father, a tender form of address, said four times in 19:42–45.

carryVoice: Your line: peace be upon you, father. Conviction and kindness, both at once. That's day four hundred seventy-three.
